title: Two Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair versus a single pass hash map lookup.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one valid answer exists, and the same element cannot be used twice.

blocks.text: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one valid answer exists, and the same element cannot be used twice.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Two Puzzle Pieces That Fit
blocks.text: Imagine a pile of puzzle pieces and a target shape formed by exactly two of them fitting together. Rather than trying every possible pair by hand, remembering which pieces have already been examined makes it possible to instantly recognize the matching piece the moment it shows up.

blocks.caption: Find the two array values whose sum equals the target, return their indices

blocks.text: The same value can appear twice in the array as long as they are different elements. Here both 3s add up to 6, and since they occupy different indices (0 and 1), the answer is [0, 1].
This problem is worth recognizing as the cleanest, most direct example of an idea already seen twice earlier in this sheet.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For any single number in the array, the only thing that actually matters is whether its complement, target minus that number, has already appeared earlier in the array, not how it compares to every other individual number.

Observation 2: This is exactly the same "have I seen this before" question already answered with a hash set for Happy Number, and with a hash map for Fraction to Recurring Decimal, just asking about a computed complement instead of a repeated value or remainder.

Observation 3: Testing nums equal to [2, 7, 11, 15] with target 9 confirms it, by the time 7 is reached, its complement, 2, has already been recorded, so the pair is found the instant 7 is examined, with no need to look back through the array.

Observation 4: A hash map from value to index answers "has this exact complement been seen, and if so, at which index" in one constant time operation, collapsing a pairwise comparison into a single pass.
Naming this explicitly as the same remember-and-check pattern already used twice before is what makes the hash map solution the obvious next step rather than something to search for from scratch.
Check every possible pair of indices, adding the two values and comparing the sum against target.

items: For every index i from 0 to n minus 1, look at every index j after i.
Add nums[i] and nums[j].
If the sum equals target, return [i, j].

blocks.caption: Brute force: check the sum of every pair of indices

codes.python:
def two_sum(nums, target):
    n = len(nums)
    for i in range(n):                                     # try every index as the first number
        for j in range(i + 1, n):                            # try every later index as the second number
            if nums[i] + nums[j] == target:
                return [i, j]                                    # found the matching pair
    return []


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [2, 7, 11, 15]
    target = 9
    print(two_sum(nums, target))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop always starts at i plus 1, never revisiting an earlier index or pairing an index with itself, so every pair is checked exactly once.
The sum is compared directly against target with no intermediate storage, since nothing about this pair needs to be remembered once it fails to match.
The function returns the instant a match is found, so no unnecessary pairs are checked once the one valid answer has been located.

blocks.text: This checks every possible pair, so it is guaranteed to find the one valid answer if it exists.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), for the two nested loops over every pair.
Space: O(1), no extra data structure is used.

Limitation: most of these pair comparisons are wasted work. For each number, what actually matters is whether its complement, target minus that number, has already been seen, not comparing it against every other number one at a time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every pair works but is wasteful: for a given number, only one specific other value, its complement, could ever complete a valid pair, yet every other number gets compared against it anyway.

What stays the same as Happy Number and Fraction to Recurring Decimal: the underlying idea, remember what has already been encountered, then check a hash structure directly instead of scanning.

What is different here: the value being checked is a computed complement, target minus the current number, rather than the current number or remainder itself.

Can a hash map answer both "has the complement been seen" and "at what index" in one step: yes, mapping value to index serves both purposes with a single lookup.

The core idea: walk the array once, and for every number, check the hash map for its complement before recording the current number, so an element is never paired with itself.

Walk through the array once, and for each value, first check whether its complement, target minus the current value, has already been recorded. If it has, the answer is found immediately. If not, record the current value and its index before moving on. A hash map gives constant time average lookups and insertions, turning the pairwise search into a single pass.
Keep a hash map from value to index. For each number, check the map for its complement before inserting the current number, so the same element is never paired with itself.

blocks.caption: Optimized: one pass, checking the hash map for the complement before storing

blocks.text: This works because checking the map for the complement happens before the current value is stored, so a number can never be paired with itself, and because the map only ever needs to hold values from earlier in the scan, if the complement for the current number exists anywhere in the array, it is guaranteed to already be in the map by the time it is needed, since the problem guarantees exactly one valid pair exists.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant time average hash map operations.
Space: O(n), for the hash map, which in the worst case stores nearly every element.

blocks.text: This problem is the standard introduction to trading space for time: a single hash map turns an O(n squared) pairwise search into a linear scan, and this exact pattern (remember what has been seen, check a computed complement) reappears throughout array and string problems that ask for a pair, a subarray, or a substring matching some condition.

items: Inserting the current value into the map before checking for its complement, which would incorrectly let an element pair with itself.
Returning the values themselves instead of their indices, which is what the problem actually asks for.
Assuming the array is sorted. It is not, so index order in the answer does not need to match value order.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every pair", think: remember what has been seen and check for a computed complement, exactly like Happy Number's cycle detection.
If the interviewer says "what if the array were sorted", think: a two pointer approach solves this in O(n) time and O(1) extra space instead.
If the interviewer says "what if there were multiple valid pairs", think: the same hash map approach extends naturally, collecting every match instead of returning on the first one.

Three Sum and Four Sum, which extend this same idea to more numbers, often combined with sorting and two pointers instead of a pure hash map.
Subarray Sum Equals K, which reuses this exact complement-in-a-hash-map idea, just applied to running prefix sums instead of individual values.
Any problem asking for a pair, subarray, or substring satisfying a sum or difference condition, where a hash map of previously seen values or prefixes is almost always the fastest approach.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: the complement-lookup pattern, remembering every value seen so far in a hash map so the value still needed to complete a pair can be checked in constant time.

Core Idea: for each number, check whether its complement, target minus that number, is already in a hash map before recording the current number, turning a pairwise comparison into a single linear pass.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized version.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized version, to hold the hash map.
Most Important Observation: this is the purest form of "have I seen this before", checking a computed complement instead of a raw repeated value.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the brute force; immediately reaching for a hash map and correctly ordering the check-then-insert steps is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: check the complement in the map first, then store the current value, one pass, one hash map.
